set.statement: In people born from 1950 to 1993 and adopted in Sweden outside their biological family (adoptions by relatives or by a biological parent's partner excluded), with register information on both adoptive parents and at least one biological parent, both what was passed on from their biological parents and features of the adoptive home they grew up in were associated with a later register record of drug problems; the study estimated no heritability percentage. Of 18,115 adoptees followed in national registers to 2009 (a record meant a diagnosis of a drug use disorder or drug psychosis in hospital, outpatient, primary-care or death records; a conviction under two crime-register codes for crimes related to drug abuse, convictions only for alcohol-related crimes or only for drug trafficking or possession not counting; or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives, hypnotics or opioids; alcohol and tobacco excluded; the study calls this 'drug abuse'), 4.5% had a record, against 2.9% of everyone in Sweden born in the same years. Adoptees whose biological parent had a record, though they were not raised by that parent, had one in 8.6% of cases against 4.2% when neither biological parent had (odds ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.66 to 2.62), and in 11.9% when both had; records were also shared with biological siblings raised apart (full siblings, odds ratio 1.84, 1.28 to 2.64; half siblings, 1.41, 1.19 to 1.67). In the adoptive home, records were shared with adoptive siblings, who were not biologically related to the adoptee: 6.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees with a record had one, against 3.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees without (odds ratio 1.95, 1.43 to 2.65), and the adoptive mother's divorce and an adoptive parent's death were also associated with a record; adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with a record had one in 6.8% of cases against 4.5%, an imprecise estimate that included no difference (1.55, 0.86 to 2.80), with only 1.0% of adoptive parents affected. On the scale of absolute risk, an adverse adoptive home added more risk for adoptees whose biological relatives' records put them at higher risk, an interaction the paper does not report on the odds scale; at the lowest level of the biological-relative index the added risk could not be told apart from none (Kendler et al., 2012). An adoption study separates the family that passes on genes from the family that raises a child, but what passes from biological parents includes the pregnancy, care before placement (up to about 3 in 10 adoptees may have joined their adoptive family after age 5, by a census-based estimate) and how agencies matched children to homes (modest, by the authors' judgment), as well as genes. The authors report that children usually spent the time before placement in a nursery or foster home rather than with their biological parents, and that later placement did not go with a higher risk (odds ratio 0.96 per year before adjustment, 1.00 after); their argument against effects in the womb rests on 9.9% with an affected biological father against 8.2% with an affected mother, overlapping intervals without a test. As summarized, without figures, by a narrative review, twin studies find that genes and both shared and individual environment influence whether people start using tobacco, alcohol or cannabis, that genes matter more for regular use and dependence, and that the environment twins share is no longer detectable for regular use or dependence in adulthood though it is in adolescence (the adoptive-sibling association above, if it reflects the shared home, does not fit this summary well); single genetic variants have small effects that replicate poorly, scores combining many variants explained less than 1% of the variation in alcohol dependence, and the size of genetic influence has been reported to differ between environments (Prom-Wormley et al., 2017, second-hand). A heritability, where one is given, describes how much of the differences between people in one population at one time go with differences in their genes; it is not the share of any one person's risk that comes from genes (the editors' explanation; Visscher et al., 2008, on what heritability means, is not yet read). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
set.plain: Do genes and the home you grow up in shape drug problems? In a large Swedish study of adopted children, both were linked to drug problems. Children whose birth parent had a drug problem in official records had one themselves about twice as often (about 9 in 100, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did), even though other parents raised them. Drug problems were also shared within adoptive families, between children not related by birth: when an adopted child had one, about 6 in 100 of their adoptive brothers and sisters did too, against 3 in 100 when the adopted child did not. Divorce or a parent's death in the adoptive family also went with more drug problems. The study did not work out a percentage due to genes, and what comes from birth parents also includes the pregnancy and the time before adoption. A percentage due to genes, where studies give one, describes differences between people in one place and time; it does not say how much of one person's risk comes from genes.
set.population: People born 1950–1993 and adopted in Sweden outside their biological family (adoptions by relatives or by a biological parent's partner excluded), with register information on both adoptive parents and at least one biological parent, who first lived with their adoptive parents by age 10 by a census-based estimate (18,115 adoptees; national registers to 2009); twin studies summarized without figures by a narrative review
set.outcome: A register record of drug problems (the study's 'drug abuse': drug use disorder or drug psychosis diagnoses; convictions under two crime-register codes for crimes related to drug abuse, with alcohol-only, trafficking and possession convictions excluded; or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives, hypnotics or opioids; alcohol and tobacco excluded)
set.magnitude: Kendler et al. (2012): adoptees with a record 4.5% (95% CI 4.2–4.8; 820 people) vs 2.9% nationally for the same birth years. Biological parent with vs without a record 8.6% vs 4.2%, OR 2.09 (1.66–2.62); none, one or both biological parents 4.2%, 8.2%, 11.9%; biological father 9.9% (7.2–12.1), mother 8.2% (6.3–10.5). Biological full siblings raised apart, record in 10.7% of the full siblings of adoptees with a record vs 6.1% of those of adoptees without, OR 1.84 (1.28–2.64); half siblings 7.4% vs 5.3%, OR 1.41 (1.19–1.67). Adoptive siblings of adoptees with vs without a record 6.2% vs 3.2%, OR 1.95 (1.43–2.65); adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with vs without a record 6.8% vs 4.5%, OR 1.55 (0.86–2.80). Multivariable: adoptive mother's divorce OR 1.31 (1.03–1.68), adoptive parent's death 1.37 (1.08–1.73). Interaction on the probability scale 0.0005 per decile × decile (0.0001–0.0008): each decile of the adoptive-home index added about 0.15 percentage points of risk at the lowest decile of the biological-relative index (the main effect with the interaction term, 0.0015, −0.0006 to 0.0036, an interval that includes no added risk) and about 0.6 at the highest (editors' calculation on the study card, recomputed with deciles coded 0 to 9). Later placement: odds ratio 0.96 per year before adjustment, 1.00 after. No heritability estimated. As summarized by Prom-Wormley et al. (2017): polygenic scores explained less than 1% of the variance in alcohol dependence; no twin heritability figure for any drug use disorder is given.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Rated as worded: Swedish adoptees born 1950–1993 with a biological parent in the registers (the paper does not say 'born in Sweden' or 'domestic adoptions') and a broad register construct, both stated; the gap to diagnosed use disorders, to other countries and to later cohorts is stated, not assumed away.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational (a national register adoption cohort): starts low; not downgraded. Strict reading: counting the broad register outcome and the possibly too narrow sibling intervals as risk of bias would give very low. The gradient with the number of affected biological parents (4.2%, 8.2%, 11.9%) is not used as a dose–response upgrade: it concerns the biological side only, cannot separate genes from the pregnancy and care before placement, and the claim's weaker link, the adoptive home, shows no gradient (the adoptive-parent estimate is imprecise). No heritability percentage was estimated, the extreme-decile odds ratios in the paper overstate the contrast by one step and are not used (card reporting issue), and the gene-environment interaction holds on the probability scale only as reported, with the added risk at the lowest biological-relative level not distinguishable from none. The narrative review gives no figures for drug use disorders and is used for context only (second-hand). The statement that a heritability is not the share of one person's risk is the editors' explanation; the paper the round lists on this point (Visscher et al., 2008) is not yet read. Status single study.

evidence_set: National register adoption cohort: 18,115 Swedish adoptees born 1950–1993 who first lived with their adoptive parents by age 10 (12,783 by age 5), linked to 78,079 biological parents and siblings and 51,208 adoptive parents and siblings; adoptees 52.2% male; mean age at last information 46.2 years; mean age at first living with adoptive parents 4.4 years; registers covering 1961–2009. Inclusion (Sample): people born 1950–1993 who had been adopted, with register information on both adoptive parents and at least one biological parent; adoptions by biological relatives or by an adoptive parent living with a biological parent excluded (the paper does not say 'born in Sweden'). Ages at first living with the adoptive parents are estimated from 5-yearly censuses and are upper limits of the true age.

Checks for contact before placement: age at first living with adoptive parents (a census-based upper limit) was negatively associated with a record before adjustment (OR 0.96 per year, P<.01) and not associated after adjustment for the two risk indices, sex and birth year (1.00), and did not interact with the adoptive-home index (P=.88); at least 70.9% lived with their adoptive parents by age 5; before placement children were typically in a special nursery home, often with trial foster placements, rather than with their biological parents; results in the age-5 cohort described as broadly unchanged, without numbers.

evidence_add.locator: Table 6, column 'Multivariate Analysis With an Interaction Term', Environmental risk score and Interaction term rows; Figure legend (risk deciles coded 0 to 9)
evidence_add.extracted: In the probability-scale model with the interaction term, the environmental (adoptive-home) index had a main effect of 0.0015 per decile (95% CI −0.0006 to 0.0036, not significant); with deciles coded 0 to 9, this is the added risk per adoptive-home decile at the lowest biological-relative decile, and its interval includes no added risk. The interaction was 0.0005 (0.0001 to 0.0008, P<.05), so the slope at the highest biological-relative decile is 0.0015 + 9 × 0.0005 = 0.006 (editors' calculation, recomputed); the biological-relative main effect in the same model was 0.0028 (0.0010 to 0.0048).

set.statement: In one pre-registered online experiment with adults who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative, the words used to describe a person's difficulty changed some of the attitudes readers reported, but not others, and changed what they did in a pretend money task only slightly. 1,613 adults (largest age group 18 to 25; 55.9% women; 77.1% White; recruited through university research-participation schemes, Prolific and social media; country of residence not stated) were each randomly assigned to read one short story about a person called Alex. When Alex's serious trouble at home and work was said to come from increasing drug use rather than from a health concern (819 against 741 readers), readers reported wanting more social distance from Alex (standardized difference d 0.87), saw Alex as more dangerous (d 0.78) and gave higher public-stigma scores (d 0.95; means 50.6 against 42.2): two of these differences are large by the usual standard and the third (danger) is just below it. They agreed less that the condition had genetic or disease causes (d −0.35), and their hope for Alex's recovery was the same within the study's equivalence bounds (d −0.06). In a pretend task in which readers could give or take small sums of money for Alex's answers, readers of the drug-use story took slightly more money (62.05 against 53.96 pence; d 0.14, interval 0.02 to 0.26), a difference the study could not show to be larger than its 0.20 threshold for a meaningful effect, and gave the same amount within the equivalence bounds (d −0.03). Among readers of the drug-use story, calling the condition a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' rather than a 'problem' (392 against 423) made readers agree more that it had genetic or disease causes (d 0.54; the study calls this subscale blame). With the brain-disease label, social distance (d −0.20, interval −0.36 to −0.03) and public stigma (−0.18, −0.34 to −0.02) were slightly lower, and the differences in danger (−0.11) and hope (−0.07) were smaller; all four were inconclusive, so the study could not tell whether any of them was more than trivial, and the label did not reliably change the money given or taken. Framing Alex's treatment as likely to succeed rather than uncertain (the two versions also differed in whether Alex was in a treatment programme or had seen a doctor) gave inconclusive differences on every attitude measure and on money given, and the same money taken (Pennington et al., 2023). The study measured attitudes reported after one made-up story, not how people who use drugs are actually treated by the public, health workers or services; people with a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis, or a close relative with one, could not take part; in the drug-use version four questionnaire items named opioids, so that comparison changed the questions as well as the story; the intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals; and it did not compare person-first words with labels for the person. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), a randomized study of two commonly used terms for people with substance-related conditions, is not yet read. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
set.plain: Do words about drug use change how others see a person? In one experiment, 1,613 adults online each read one short story about a person called Alex, with the wording chosen at random. When Alex's trouble was said to come from drug use rather than a health concern, readers clearly wanted to keep more distance from Alex, saw Alex as more dangerous and gave higher stigma scores. In a pretend money task they also took slightly more money from Alex, a small difference the study could not call meaningful. Calling it a 'brain disease' instead of a 'problem' made readers think more that it came from genes or illness. Readers also kept slightly less distance, but the study could not tell whether this or the label's other effects mattered. Readers rated a made-up story; people with a drug or mental health diagnosis, or a close relative with one, could not take part; and the study did not test words for the person, such as person-first words.
set.population: Adults recruited online (university research-participation schemes, Prolific, social media; country of residence not stated; largest age group 18–25) who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative; 1,613 randomized
set.exposure: Reading a short story in which a person's difficulty was described as drug use (against a health concern); within the drug-use story, as a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' (against a 'problem'); and treatment framed as likely to succeed, with Alex in a treatment programme (against uncertain, with Alex having seen a doctor)
set.magnitude: Pennington et al. (2023), Cohen's d with intervals printed as 99% that match 98% intervals (card reporting issue): drug use vs health concern (819 vs 741): social distance 0.87 (0.74 to 0.99), perceived danger 0.78 (0.66 to 0.90), public stigma 0.95 (0.82 to 1.07; means 50.59 vs 42.15), blame subscale (genetic or disease attribution) −0.35 (−0.47 to −0.23), all meaningful by the study's rule; prognostic optimism −0.06 (equivalent); continued care 0.09 (inconclusive); reward −0.03 (equivalent; 248.11 vs 249.72 pence); punishment 0.14 (0.02 to 0.26; inconclusive: the interval does not include zero but reaches below the 0.20 bound; 62.05 vs 53.96 pence). 'Chronically relapsing brain disease' vs 'problem' (392 vs 423, drug-use arm): blame subscale 0.54 (0.38 to 0.71; means 8.61 vs 7.22), meaningful; continued care 0.01 (equivalent); social distance −0.20 (−0.36 to −0.03), prognostic optimism −0.07, danger −0.11, public stigma −0.18 (−0.34 to −0.02; means 49.62 vs 51.20) and reward 0.15, all inconclusive; punishment 0.007 (equivalent). Treatment framed as likely to succeed vs uncertain (383 vs 362): every self-report measure and reward inconclusive (for example public stigma 0.31, 0.14 to 0.48, higher with the uncertain framing), punishment equivalent. Detectable equivalence bounds ±0.28 and ±0.30 for the label and treatment comparisons.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: One study. The authors say two earlier vignette studies agree that drug problems are among the most stigmatized conditions, but as the paper describes them only Rundle et al. (2021) compared a substance use disorder with other conditions; Kelly et al. (2021) had no comparison condition. The two disagree on the brain-disease label, partly because they used different measures.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: A young online convenience sample without substance use or psychiatric diagnoses in themselves or close relatives, one hypothetical story, and self-reported attitudes and a pretend money task instead of how people who use drugs are treated; the words tested describe the condition, not the person, so person-first wording was not tested.
set.grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. The verb increases rests on random assignment within the experiment; the rating concerns how far the result carries to other people, other words and real treatment. The intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals (all 24, recomputed from Table 1) and one p value is printed as below .01 when it is about .011 (card reporting issues); the study's classifications do not change. Three differences classed as inconclusive have printed intervals that do not include zero (money taken with the drug-use story; social distance and public stigma with the brain-disease label; at 99% the public-stigma interval would reach zero), and the statement gives them as small differences rather than as no change. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), the randomized study of terms for the person, is not yet read and could add the person-first comparison this study lacks. Status single study.

evidence_set: 1,613 adults (1,622 recruited; 9 excluded) from university research-participation schemes (SONA), Prolific and social media were randomized to one of eight story conditions; largest age band 18–25 years (36.5%), 55.9% women, 77.1% White; people with their own or a close relative's substance use or psychiatric diagnosis were not eligible.

Within the drug-use arm, treatment framed as likely to succeed or as uncertain (383 vs 362) gave only inconclusive differences on every self-report measure (for example public stigma d=.31, .14 to .48, higher with the uncertain framing) and on rewards; punishments equivalent; 102 participants failed this manipulation check. The 'likely to succeed' version also said Alex was now in a treatment programme and the 'uncertain' version that Alex had visited a doctor, and the manipulation check asked about this setting.
Results › Research Question 3, 1st paragraph; Table 1, RQ3 columns; Method › Manipulation and Attention Checks; vignette (image) under Method › Measures › Vignette Development

The authors conclude that problematic substance use is among the most stigmatized health conditions and say that two earlier vignette studies concur, although as the paper describes them only Rundle et al. (2021) compared a substance use disorder with other conditions and Kelly et al. (2021) had no comparison condition; they conclude that the effects of the brain-disease label remain mixed and that aggregated and multidimensional stigma measures lead to different conclusions; their proposal that the concept is used to assign or displace responsibility depending on context was not tested.
Discussion, 2nd and 6th paragraphs; Conclusions; Introduction, 4th and 6th paragraphs
